claims.text: Context an agent loads to work on the compiler: research.md is about 2,400 words; forgetti 0.8 src is about 3,700 lines (roughly 35k tokens); the corpus is 15 files under 40 lines each.

Prior art outside the lab: React Compiler 1.0 (released 2025-10-07) builds a control-flow IR, infers mutation and aliasing effects, and groups values into reactive scopes over one flat cache from useMemoCache. Million Lint and forgetti 0.8 work on the AST without a mutation model.

claims.text: Pipeline of five phases, each a pure function from source ranges to a plan, with magic-string only in the last. 1 parse and scope (oxc-parser, finds components and hooks). 2 eligibility (per-component bailout on Rules of React breaks). 3 ownership (classifies each local value). 4 cache-tree plan (nodes, slots, dependency sets). 5 emit (magic-string inserts slot code at original ranges, no AST rewrite, no outlining). The runtime is one small cache hook.

evidence.detail: Same stack ships a multi-pass analyze-then-edit compiler: each pass reparses and edits with MagicString, chaining source maps. Benchmarks in benchmarks.md show it works at scale (up to 35.5% gzip reduction on kobalte).

claims.text: Phase 3 uses a local ownership lattice instead of an effect-and-alias IR. Each local is fresh (created in this render by a literal, array, object or known-pure constructor), frozen (fresh and past its last mutation), or opaque (props, state, hook results, use() results, anything that escaped into an unknown call). Mutating calls and writes (push, assignment to a member, passing to an unknown function) move a fresh value toward its last-mutation point. A slot may hold only a frozen or pure-derived value. A fresh value that is read after a mutation joins the dependency set of the mutating statements. This fixes the 0.8 forloop case, where const rows = [] was cached as a constant.

evidence.detail: J2: forloop is stale in 0.8 because push is not seen as mutation. The lattice marks rows as fresh until the loop ends, so the JSX return depends on the loop's inputs.

claims.ruling_why: superseded by P7, which adds the alias groups and bailout list O2 asked for

claims.text: Phase 2 and the runtime enforce the platform rules from J5. use() calls, hook results and impure statements are never given a slot, and every slot read that depends on them lists them as inputs. The cache hook is called first and unconditionally, built on useRef (not useMemo) so a discarded memo cache cannot be the only copy and a lost cache only costs a recompute. Cache init is pure for StrictMode. A component that mutates props or calls a hook conditionally is left uncompiled and reported. This fixes usectx and bailout in J2, and works on Preact 11 because it imports nothing from react/compiler-runtime.

evidence.source: research.md 'Constraints from React 19 and Preact 11'; J5
evidence.detail: useMemo may discard its cache, use() may sit in branches and must not be cached, hook order is fixed, c() is absent in Preact 11. Runtime estimate: 0.8 runtime/index.ts is part of the 3,849 lines (J7).

claims.ruling_why: upheld with the J13 write rule: inputs and value are written together after the computation returns

claims.text: Phase 4 groups values by exact dependency set, not by co-mutation scope and not one slot per expression. All values with the same input set share one compare and one slot block. Expressions whose cost is lower than one compare (a + 1, property reads of a frozen value, literals) get no slot. This targets J3: fewer slots than 0.8 (2 to 4 times more than React Compiler) and less code, while keeping 0.8's finer recompute on derived and hook, where React Compiler reruns costly('x', a) or both calls (J4).

evidence.detail: derived: RC 6 slots, 0.8 13 slots. derived/one_b: RC reruns x1,y1, 0.8 reruns y1 only. A dependency-set grouping of derived needs one slot block per input set {a}, {b}, so recompute is exact and slots stay near RC's count.

claims.text: Phase 4 keeps the tree cache. A component has a root cache. A branch (if, switch, ternary, short-circuit) and a loop or map iteration each get a child cache. JSX is cached as element values and is not outlined into memo components. An iteration cache is keyed by the JSX key or the item identity when known, by position otherwise. Child caches are created lazily, so memory is only paid for visited branches and rendered rows. This targets the map row in J4 (RC re-renders Row3 on one replaced item, 0.8 re-renders Row1) and fixes the jsxprops, earlyreturn and deepprop rows where 0.8's region-wide outlined memo re-renders children that RC does not.

evidence.detail: jsxprops/one_cls, earlyreturn/one_b, deepprop/one_other: 0.8 re-renders Child, RC does not. map/deep_item and map/append: RC Row3 and Row4, 0.8 Row1. Element caching with per-iteration caches should win both sets, to be measured.

claims.text: (soundness) A cache in useRef that is written during render is the render-purity violation React documents: a render that is discarded (Suspense, concurrent restart, StrictMode double render) can leave slot values that the next render reads as valid, so a cache keyed only by dependency compares can return output built from an uncommitted render's inputs. The claim that a lost cache only costs a recompute is true, but a polluted cache is not covered, and 0.8's useRef root is the same design. J5 notes that only useMemo's cache is discardable, and research.md leaves the StrictMode reuse question unverified. Needs a test with Suspense and transitions before P3 can claim 0 differences.

claims.text: (soundness) A local ownership lattice has no alias tracking. claims.text: Amends P2 for O2. The lattice becomes alias groups. Tracked: a group is the set of locals that may point to one fresh value. Joins come from assignment (const x = arr), a fresh value stored into a field, array element or Map/Set of another fresh value (the two groups merge), spread of a fresh value into a literal (shallow copy, new group), and a closure that references a fresh value and is created in the component (the closure joins the group, and calling it counts as a mutation of the group). Last mutation is the last statement that mutates any member of the group, so a group's slots depend on that point. Bail out the component, with a report: a fresh value passed to an unknown function or method that is not on a known-pure list, returned from a hook call, assigned to a ref.current or module variable, or captured by a closure that is passed out of the component before the group is frozen. Opaque values (props, state, hook results) are never mutated by the compiled code, and a mutation of one is a bailout, as in the bailout case in J2. The rule is sound by default: any case not on the tracked list bails out.

evidence.detail: O2 names three cases: assignment alias, field store, closure capture. Each is now tracked or bails out. Anything unlisted bails out, so the class stays closed.

claims.text: Fold J13 into the cache runtime contract in phase 5 and the runtime. A cache is a useRef object. Each slot stores its inputs and its value. A slot is written only after the computation returns, inputs and value together, so a throw leaves the slot empty and a retry recomputes. A slot read is a hit only when the slot is filled and every input is equal under Object.is. A suspended mount or an interrupted transition then matches uncompiled React.

claims.text: Amends P7 for O8. An unknown call that receives a fresh value does not bail out. Under the Rules of React the compiler may assume a render-time function does not keep a reference after it returns, so the call is treated as a mutation site: the argument group and the call result merge into one group, the call itself is never cached, and the group is frozen after the last such call. Downstream slots then depend on the group's frozen values. Bailouts shrink to the cases React Compiler also rejects or that persist a reference: mutation of props, state or hook arguments (the bailout.jsx case), a fresh value stored in ref.current or a module variable, a fresh value returned from a hook call, and a closure holding a fresh value that is passed out before the group is frozen. The cost of an unknown call is lost caching of that group, not lost compilation. No known-pure list is needed for soundness. A pure list (Math, JSON, Object.keys, array methods that do not mutate) only recovers caching.

evidence.source: evidence/out/compile-log.txt and evidence/corpus/bailout.jsx; https://react.dev/reference/rules (components and hooks must be pure; props and state are immutable)

claims.text: Answer to O9. The map file loses in J12 because of the inline element-wise compare loop, not because of the tree cache. Moving that loop into one runtime helper, keep($, i, next), which returns the stored array when every element is equal and stores next otherwise, cuts the hand map.jsx from 715 raw and 394 gzip to 594 raw and 328 gzip, which is 1.07 times React Compiler raw (554) and 1.05 times gzip (312), down from 1.29 and 1.26. The helper is one 120-byte runtime export imported once per module graph, shared by all files (rt.js is 267 bytes now, counted once, not per file; React Compiler also imports react/compiler-runtime, counted on neither side in T2). Stated threshold: over the 14 files React Compiler compiles, total gzip including one runtime import is at most 1.0 times React Compiler, and no single file is above 1.15 times. The wins in J4 and the soundness gate carry 'beat'; size is held at parity or better, as J14 allows. Not yet run for behavior, only measured for size.

claims.text: Answer to O10. One write rule, in phase 5, for every slot shape including per-row caches and grouped slots: compute the value into a local first, then write the inputs and the value together in one block after it returns. There is no cheap shape that writes inputs first. The same rule gives the keep() variant in P16 (const v = <Row/>; c[0] = item; c[1] = v). Gate: a corpus case where a slot's computation throws on its first call and succeeds on retry, for a call slot, a grouped slot and a per-row cache, each compared with uncompiled React under the T1 harness. The planner has no code path that writes before computing, so the defect cannot come from a planner choice.

evidence.detail: J13: inputs-before-value fails on throw. map.jsx wrote c[0] = item first, safe only because JSX creation cannot throw. The P16 variant uses the one rule.

claims.text: P14 says downstream slots 'depend on the group's frozen values'. A fresh group is rebuilt every render, so its identity changes each time and an Object.is compare on it never hits: every slot after an unknown call (format(rows), sortBy(items)) recomputes and its JSX re-renders, which loses to React Compiler on exactly the rows J14 counts. React Compiler keys the scope on the scope's own inputs. P14 must say the dependency set is the transitive non-fresh inputs of the group (props, state), not the group value. This is the P2 rule 'a fresh value joins the dependency set' and it is not restated in P14. Needs a corpus file with an unknown call feeding a child and a render-count gate.

evidence.source: P14 text and J14, plus evidence/out/runtime-table.txt where RC does not re-render Child on jsxprops/same
evidence.detail: Group values are created inside the render, so identity compare cannot hit. The 15-file corpus has no unknown-call-on-fresh case (P14's own grep), so no current row would catch it.

claims.ruling_why: high: a group recreated every render makes every downstream slot miss, which loses the J14 render rows

With 5 files and 1 to 3 components each, one extra bailout moves the rate by 7 to 20 points, so 'at least React Compiler's rate' cannot separate a good planner from a poor one, and RC's logger rejects many things beyond props mutation (ref reads in render, conditional hooks, globals), which P14 lists only partly. Count by component and report each difference, which P15 already does for the failing direction; raise the held-out real-shaped count to at least 10 if budget allows (about 20k tokens more, inside P9's range).

proofs.question: Does a forgetti-style cache in useRef, with each slot storing its inputs next to its value, give the same output as uncompiled React after discarded transition renders, Suspense on mount and update, and StrictMode double render?
proofs.result: value-then-inputs useRef cache matches uncompiled in all cases; inputs-then-value fails on throw and retry; 12 minutes

proofs.question: Do hand-written outputs that follow P4 (dependency-set grouping, no slot for cheap expressions) and P5 (child caches per branch and positional per iteration, cached JSX elements, no outlining) come within 1.5 times React Compiler's raw bytes on ternary, switch, map and derived, with 0 differences from uncompiled and no more re-renders than either compiler?
proofs.result: 0.73 to 1.29x RC raw bytes, 0 differences, renders tie 0.8 and beat RC on 4 rows; hand-compiled, 10 minutes

hypothesis.statement: A five-phase oxc and magic-string compiler with alias groups, a useRef tree cache, dependency-set slots and cached JSX elements is sound and beats both forgetti 0.8 and React Compiler 1.0
hypothesis.metric: on the grown corpus (at least 35 files, at least 10 held out, React 19.3 and Preact 11.2): differences from uncompiled output; total child re-renders and costly() recomputes over the runtime scenarios; gzip bytes with one runtime import; share of components compiled
hypothesis.baseline: React Compiler 1.0.0 and forgetti 0.8.5 on the 15-file corpus: 0 and 3 differences (J2), RC bytes in evidence/out/compile-table.json (J3), render rows in evidence/out/runtime-table.txt (J4), RC compiles 14 of 15
hypothesis.threshold: 0 differences on every file and both targets; total re-renders plus recomputes strictly below each compiler, and no file above the better of the two; total gzip at most 1.0x React Compiler and no file above 1.15x; compiled share at least React Compiler's on the held-out files
hypothesis.kill: any difference from uncompiled output that cannot be fixed without bailing out more components than React Compiler; or total gzip above 1.3x React Compiler after S3; or spend above 800k tokens before S4
